samasa.sense: Kubera, the god of wealth (compare कौबेरेण in 2.16)

samasa.type: tṛtīyā tatpuruṣa (महामणि a karmadhāraya, महान् चासौ मणिः च)

morph.note: A litotes: ‘not empty of wine’ means ‘always full’. The thing it is not empty of is in the instrumental (सुरया).
Accusative, though it stands beside the nominatives शेषः … सर्वनागेशः: it anticipates नागहारम्, the object in the next verse.

mantras.anvaya: धनाधिपः सुरया अशून्यं पानपात्रं ददौ। सर्वनागेशः शेषः च महामणिविभूषितं (नागहारं तस्यै ददौ)।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line is complete. The second line begins a sentence finished in 2.31: Śeṣa is its subject, and the accusative adjective waits for its noun नागहारम्.
mantras.lit: The Lord of Wealth gave a drinking-cup never empty of wine. And Śeṣa, the lord of all serpents, (gave) a … adorned with great jewels
mantras.tr: Kubera, Lord of Wealth, gave her a drinking-cup never empty of wine; and Śeṣa, king of all serpents, a jewel-studded
mantras.tr_note: The second line runs into 2.31, where the noun (नागहारम्) and the verb stand.

comm.t: Kubera, keeper of the gods’ treasure, gives a cup that is never empty of wine. The cup returns in battle: before slaying Mahiṣa she drinks and says ‘Roar, roar for a moment, fool, while I drink the honey-wine’ (3.38).

The wine-vessel is among the eighteen objects of the madhyama-carita dhyāna (सुराभाजनम्, Gita Press pāṭha). In the Śākta tradition the cup is commonly read as the Goddess’s exhilaration in battle, not as an ordinary indulgence; the text itself says only what is given.

samasa.type: karmadhāraya (of identification: the serpent is the necklace)
samasa.sense: a necklace that is a serpent, given by the serpent-king
samasa.alt: Also ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa, नागानां हारः ‘the necklace of the Nāgas’ — a jewelled necklace from their treasury. महामणिविभूषितम् (2.30) fits either: Nāgas are known for the jewels on their hoods.

morph.note: Present ātmanepada of √धा: reduplicated दध्- + ते, with the aspiration moved forward to the first syllable (दध् + ते → धत्ते). The present tense describes Śeṣa’s permanent office: he who bears this earth.
The nominative here is the subject of the next verse’s सम्मानिता … ननाद; the instrumentals सुरैः, भूषणैः, आयुधैः are the agent and the means of that participle.

mantras.anvaya: यः इमां पृथिवीं धत्ते, (सः शेषः) तस्यै नागहारं ददौ। अन्यैः अपि सुरैः भूषणैः तथा आयुधैः देवी (सम्मानिता)।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line closes the sentence begun in 2.30 with a relative clause on Śeṣa. The second line opens a new sentence whose participle and verb (सम्मानिता … ननाद) stand in 2.32.
mantras.lit: serpent-necklace he gave to her — he who bears this earth. By other gods too, with ornaments and with weapons likewise, the Goddess —
mantras.tr: serpent-necklace — Śeṣa, who bears this earth. And the Goddess, honoured by the other gods as well with ornaments and weapons,
mantras.tr_note: The second line is completed by सम्मानिता in 2.32; ‘honoured’ is brought forward for English order.

comm.t: Śeṣa, the serpent who holds up the earth, gives a jewelled serpent-necklace. Then the list is closed with a summary: the other gods too honoured her with ornaments and weapons.

Śākta readers see in the catalogue of gifts (2.20–31) the gods handing back to the Goddess powers that are hers: several weapons are drawn out of the gods’ own weapons (2.20–23), as her body was drawn out of their light (2.13–18).

morph.note: Perfect of √नद् with reduplication न-नाद (the root vowel lengthened in the 3rd singular). The same root gives नाद ‘roar’ in the next line.
Past participle of the causative stem पूरय- (‘to fill’) with आ ‘completely’. It is a passive participle used as a finite verb: ‘(the sky) was filled’.

mantras.anvaya: (अन्यैः अपि सुरैः भूषणैः आयुधैः तथा) सम्मानिता (देवी) साट्टहासं मुहुः मुहुः उच्चैः ननाद। तस्याः घोरेण नादेन कृत्स्नं नभः आपूरितम्।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two sentences: the first finishes 2.31b (देवी … सम्मानिता ननाद); the second is passive, with the roar as agent.
mantras.lit: honoured, roared loudly with loud laughter again and again. By her terrible roar the whole sky was filled.
mantras.tr: roared aloud again and again, with peals of laughter. The whole sky was filled with her terrible roar.

comm.t: Armed and adorned, the Goddess’s first act is a roar mixed with laughter. The roar fills the sky; the next two verses follow its effect through the worlds.
Her laughter in the face of battle is a recurring mark of this carita: she fights without effort and is unwearied (अनायस्तानना, 2.50). Laughter here shows sovereignty, not mockery.

morph.note: Instrumental of a negated present participle: ‘(by the roar) not being contained’, i.e. a sound that no space could hold. It and अतिमहता qualify the roar of 2.32, which is not repeated.
Perfect 3rd plural of √क्षुभ्: reduplication चु- (k → c in the reduplicating syllable) + क्षुभ् + -उः.
Perfect 3rd plural ātmanepada (-इरे) of √कम्प्; contrast parasmaipada चुक्षुभुः beside it.

mantras.anvaya: अमायता अतिमहता (नादेन) महान् प्रतिशब्दः अभूत्। सकलाः लोकाः चुक्षुभुः, समुद्राः च चकम्पिरे।
mantras.anvaya_en: Three clauses: the echo caused by the roar (instrumental of cause), the worlds shaken, the seas trembling.
mantras.lit: By the uncontainable, exceedingly great (roar) a mighty echo arose. All the worlds were shaken, and the oceans trembled.
mantras.tr: From that boundless, immense roar a mighty echo rang out; all the worlds were shaken and the oceans trembled.

comm.t: The roar is too great to be held anywhere; its echo sets the worlds and oceans shaking. The effects are listed outward: sky (2.32), worlds and seas (2.33), earth and mountains (2.34).
The roar is the first sign the asuras receive of her: it is this sound that Mahiṣa rushes towards in 2.37 (अभ्यधावत तं शब्दम्).

flags.uncertain: अमायता is taken as the instrumental of a negated present participle (‘uncontainable’). The same letters can be divided अमायत अतिमहता, with अमायत an imperfect ātmanepada of √मा (‘it was measured / contained’); but that leaves the clause without a negative and without a clear subject, so the participle reading is followed.

samasa.sense: the mountains, which hold the earth firm

samasa.literal: she who travels by a lion
samasa.sense: the lion-rider — the lion just given by Himavat (2.29)
samasa.alt: Often glossed as सिंहः वाहनं यस्याः सा, a bahuvrīhi ‘she whose mount is a lion’; strictly that analysis gives सिंहवाहना, and the -इनी ending marks the upapada formation.

morph.note: Perfect 3rd plural of √चल् without reduplication: a root of the shape C-a-C with a single consonant on each side substitutes e for a and drops the reduplication in the weak forms (चेलुः, not *चचलुः). Contrast the singular चचाल at the start of the line.
Perfect 3rd plural of √वच् with samprasāraṇa: व → उ, and the reduplicated उ + उ gives ऊ (ऊचुः ‘they said’); compare उवाच.
Imperative 2nd singular of √जि on the stem जय-: the acclamation ‘Be victorious!’, quoted with इति.

mantras.anvaya: वसुधा चचाल, सकलाः महीधराः च चेलुः। देवाः च मुदा तां सिंहवाहिनीं ‘जय’ इति ऊचुः।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two clauses of upheaval, then the gods’ acclamation: ‘जय’ इति is the quoted word, ताम् the person addressed.
mantras.lit: The earth shook, and all the mountains quaked. And the gods with joy said ‘Be victorious!’ to her, the lion-rider.
mantras.tr: The earth shook and all the mountains quaked, and the gods cried out in joy to the lion-rider, ‘Victory to you!’
mantras.tr_note: ‘Victory to you’ renders the imperative जय (‘be victorious’).

comm.t: The roar reaches the earth and the mountains, and the gods answer it with one word: जय. सिंहवाहिनी is the first epithet the gods give her after her arming.

जय, ‘be victorious’, is at once an acclamation and a prayer. The same imperative is the refrain of the Argalā Stotra recited before the text in the Gita Press pāṭha (जय त्वं देवि चामुण्डे …), a separate liturgical hymn.
